session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the routines, habits, preferences, and social worlds that shape what they eat. I will not foreground gender or masculinity explicitly in the framing; I will let those themes emerge from the discussion itself. The collective identity I'll invite them to speak from is simply: men talking honestly about food and the people and places in their lives.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food identity (Section 3): This is the most sensitive area. Participants are older UK men — social desirability pressure may produce deflection ('it doesn't really affect me'). Behavioural grounding and concrete example probes will be essential. Watch for contradictions between stated attitudes and described behaviours.

Plant-based eating as a personal prospect (Section 4): Participants are predominantly meat eaters (3 of 4). This section carries high consensus risk — the group may converge on barriers quickly without genuine differentiation. Sharpening moves and dissent invitations may be needed.

Social context and peer influence (Sections 1–3): Understanding how male friendship shapes food choices requires moving from abstract opinion to specific remembered events and named places. The risk is participants describing the social norm rather than their own experience.

What would make plant-based eating more appealing (Section 5): Answers here may be performative or hypothetical. Probing for specificity — actual foods, actual contexts, actual social conditions — will require persistent but light-touch follow-up.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Fletcher is 64, rural Scotland, confirmed meat eater. May have strong opinions tied to regional and rural identity — farming, local food culture, traditional Scottish diet. Possible dominant voice if he has strong views; worth monitoring. Rural identity may be a useful anchor for specificity probes.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Watch for rural/regional identity framing that forecloses exploration — e.g. 'that's just how things are up here'. Probe for the personal underneath the cultural.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Keith is 72, suburban North West, flexitarian — the only participant who already moderates his meat consumption. He is a potential outlier in the group, which creates both a research asset (genuine experience of dietary change) and a social risk (others may defer to or dismiss him as the 'health-conscious one'). May be quieter if he anticipates pushback.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Ensure Keith's flexitarian experience is genuinely explored, not just noted and moved on from. His position makes him uniquely placed to speak to Sections 4 and 5. Also monitor whether the group subtly marginalises his perspective.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Patrick is 73, suburban South East, meat eater. Age and location suggest possibly traditional views on food. May frame food choices in terms of habit, health, or practicality rather than social identity. Hard to anticipate engagement style from profile alone.

Toby is 68, rural South West, meat eater. Rural identity similar to Fletcher — may share framing around local produce, outdoor lifestyle, farming connections. Could align strongly with Fletcher, creating a dominant rural-meat-eating bloc. Worth separating their voices when possible.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: If Toby and Fletcher align early, use redirect_to_group or direct_probe on Patrick and Keith to prevent the conversation being dominated by a rural-traditional consensus.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender: All four participants are older men. Direct questions about gender and identity may produce deflection or 'it doesn't apply to me' responses. Plan behavioural grounding early — move from attitudes to specific remembered moments.

Consensus risk on plant-based barriers: Three confirmed meat eaters plus one flexitarian may converge quickly on 'I could never give up meat' without differentiation. Have a sharpening move ready for Section 4 (e.g. asking what specifically would make it easier rather than whether they would do it at all).

Keith's flexitarian status as group outlier: He may self-censor or be talked over. Monitor his participation across Sections 4 and 5 especially — his lived experience is highly relevant and may need active protection.

Rural/traditional identity as a shield: Fletcher and Toby may invoke regional or lifestyle identity to close down exploration rather than open it up. Treat regional specificity as a starting point for probing, not an endpoint.

Homogeneous age cohort: All participants are 64–73. Generational food norms (meat as 'proper dinner', plant-based as a young person's trend) may produce unchallenged shared assumptions. Be prepared to invite dissent or introduce mild sharpening when these surface.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro and male friendship): Hold back. Light facilitation, minimal probing. Goal is rapport and warm-up, not depth. Let participants set the tone. Section 2 (everyday food decision-making): Moderate directivity. Move from abstract ('I just eat what I fancy') to behavioural specifics. Use one or two concrete grounding probes but don't exhaust the topic — it scaffolds Sections 3–5. Section 3 (gender and food): Push harder here. This is the section most vulnerable to deflection. Use behavioural grounding, contradiction surfacing, and dissent invitations actively. Don't accept the first 'it doesn't really' response without a follow-up. Sections 4–5 (plant-based shift and appeal): Push hardest. These sections carry the core research value. Differentiation between participants matters — avoid letting any single framing dominate. Keith's flexitarian experience should be drawn out explicitly if it hasn't emerged naturally. Section 6 (closing): Light touch again. Brief, warm, allow participants to add anything they felt was missing.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive approximately 60% of the total budget combined, reflecting their research primacy. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocations to allow genuine warm-up and scaffolding without crowding out the core discussion. Intro and closing sections receive the minimum necessary for function — ground rules, introductions, and a brief close.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This introductory section centered on place-based identity and the cumulative erosion of rural community infrastructure. A strong theme emerged around service closures — post offices, GP surgeries — not merely as practical inconveniences but as catalysts for social fragmentation and demographic decline. Participants framed these losses as interconnected and self-reinforcing rather than isolated events. Rootedness and resistance to relocation were prominent counterweights to the logic of 'just move closer to services.'
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was orienting participants and establishing geographic diversity before moving to substantive content. I let the rural participants' organic exchange develop without interruption, then intervened to draw in Keith, who had been silent. The direct address worked — he contributed a useful suburban counterpoint. The closing pivot to the core topic question was clean and well-timed, arriving once all voices had been introduced and a natural conversational rhythm had formed.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the pub as a social anchor, but quickly complicated that framing: the space associated with ease and belonging was revealed to carry implicit norms — around food, masculinity, what counts as 'normal' — that can quietly exclude. The dominant theme was invisible social pressure: not overt hostility but ambient expectation that some participants navigate by withdrawal rather than confrontation. Gathering spaces weren't just closing; they were narrowing.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: This section was largely unmoderated — Patrick and Keith developed a genuine exchange organically, and I held back to let it run. The intervention came at the natural exhaustion point of their dialogue, using Keith's own phrase as a bridging device before redirecting to a more grounded, practical question. The pivot aimed to prevent the conversation from becoming abstract too early. It felt well-timed; the organic exchange had done the work of surfacing the tension without my needing to engineer it.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section complicated the earlier theme of ambient social pressure by introducing a geographic variable: whether the 'backdrop' of food culture feels constraining depends on context — thick local familiarity versus wider cultural norms. The key tension was between banter-as-harm and structure-as-harm, with Toby's resistance gradually softening into a genuine acknowledgement that systemic assumptions can narrow belonging without anyone acting badly. Invisible pressure was reframed not as interpersonal hostility but as environmental default.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back almost entirely while Toby and Keith negotiated a real disagreement that resolved productively without my intervention. The section ended on a moment of genuine mutual concession — exactly the kind of shift worth preserving before moving on. The pivot question on gender and food was deliberately kept open and personal, aiming to personalise what had become slightly abstract without closing off the structural thread Keith had been developing.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier theme of invisible structural pressure by introducing the concept of positional comfort: those who conform to the default are insulated from its costs and therefore blind to its operation. The dominant movement was participants recognising, in real time, that not experiencing pressure as pressure is itself a form of privilege — and that passive non-challenge functions as active maintenance of the norm. The familiar became newly legible as a constraint.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back almost entirely while Fletcher and Patrick developed a genuinely reflexive exchange that didn't need steering. My two interventions were targeted reintegrations — bringing Keith in to receive what had been said about him, then Toby to prevent his earlier scepticism from silting over. Both worked: Keith's response was measured and precise; Toby's concession was credible rather than performed. The section closing felt earned.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section shifted from invisible social pressure to the practical and motivational anatomy of dietary change. Participants distinguished between structural barriers (geographic infrastructure, cooking knowledge, social inconvenience) and the more honest admission that comfort, not incapacity, is the real obstacle. A productive tension emerged between Keith's willingness to accept awkwardness as part of change-making and the others' candid acknowledgement that the motivational pull simply isn't there — reframing 'can't' as 'prefer not to.'
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back through the Keith-Patrick exchange, which was generating genuine and productive friction without needing steering. My two interventions were geographic reintegrations — drawing in Fletcher and Toby to test whether rural infrastructure added a materially different dimension. Both confirmed the motivational gap was the real story, not just access. The closing pivot toward appeal and desirability was designed to move the group from honest self-assessment toward something more constructive and forward-facing.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section turned on a single recursive move: participants dismantling their own stated barriers in real time. The appeal-versus-access distinction opened a crack, and Fletcher's unprompted self-correction — 'that's not a fact, that's a choice' — pulled the others through it. Toby and Patrick followed in quick succession. Keith's account then introduced a compound model: change required both the food being genuinely good and caring about something larger than the food itself.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back almost entirely through the Fletcher-Toby-Patrick cascade, which had its own momentum and didn't need steering. The two targeted interventions — opening the appeal question to the group, then isolating Keith as the one participant with lived experience of change — were designed to bookend what the others had surfaced with a concrete counterexample. Both worked. Keith's response gave the section a structurally different ending without repositioning him as exemplar.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section moved from structural and motivational analysis toward something quieter: the possibility of self-attentiveness as an entry point to change. The dominant theme was the gap between noticing — bodily signals, habitual patterns — and acting on what's noticed. Rather than resolving into commitment, the section ended in honest suspension: an acknowledgement that a different question exists, without the pull to answer it.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: This was a single-turn closing reflection from Toby followed by a wrap. There was nothing to steer — the section was Toby integrating the session's arc on his own terms. My only role was a clean, warm close that acknowledged the group's candour without inflating it. That felt right: the session had earned a quiet ending, and adding a final moderator question would have diluted what Toby had just done.
